newsitem.title: UK: All eyes in metals watch "powder keg" copper.
newsitem.headline: All eyes in metals watch "powder keg" copper.

text.p: A potentially explosive mix of bullish factors could trigger another sharp rise in copper prices between now and the end of the year, extending a vigorous rally that has been seen this week.
Traders said physical supply tightness and open positions in futures and options threaten to launch a market that is already up 17 percent in three weeks to a higher range, albeit briefly.
"You've got to be careful of copper. It could get explosive," said one senior physical copper merchant.
"We believe that copper prices still have considerable upside in the near term," Macquarie Equities said in a report earlier in the week.
They forecast cash copper to rise as high as $1.20 per pound ($2,646/tonne), 11 percent above current levels.
Benchmark three months copper futures on the London Metal Exchange (LME) hit a five-month high of $2,232 a tonne on Tuesday, up from $1,900 as recently as October 30.
The cash premium over three month values has also flared to around $160 a tonne against around $35 at the end of October.

Prices are at the highest since June 14 when Sumitomo Corp sacked star trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging that the architect of a high price copper trading strategy was a maverick who lost it $2.6 billion in unauthorized deals. The main fundamental factor driving prices and spreads higher is low global stocks.

On Tuesday inventories held in LME-supervised warehouses fell below 100,000 tonnes for the first time since 1990. Total reported global stocks equate to under four weeks' demand, a level analysts describe as critical.

Last week the market was unsettled by reports of huge unreported stocks possibly lying in Rotterdam. But physical copper traders have been quick to play down the possibility of large "hidden" stocks in Europe or anywhere else.

Concern that China may export large tonnages into LME warehouses in Singapore has also faded following reports that China's state reserve has bought more metal than expected to use in huge infrastructure projects during the next few years.
"I would say some 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes of metal have been shipped there and there could be more," said a trader.
Adding to physical supply tightness is strong copper demand in the U.S. and Far East and a slight pick-up in Europe.
And as well as being tight fundamentally, the market looks tight technically, LME traders explained.
Large short positions in LME futures still lie open between now and the end of the year, despite evidence of heavy fund short-covering late last week.

Because short positions are several times bigger than total LME copper stocks traders are wary of price spikes. Short position holders may try to buy back positions to avoid having to deliver physical material when the contracts expire.
But sellers of physical copper, and futures are scarce.
"There is a large bubble of open interest between now and December," a physical trader said. "A lot still has to be unwound into very little volume."
Some traders have questioned whether the one percent limit the LME put on the cost of borrowing cash copper for one day in May should be in place.
Based on Tuesday's prices the limit is indicated at around $23 a tonne a day, way below current market quotes. But nearby spreads could easily flare, traders warned.
"The limit was put on when stocks were 300,000 tonnes or so, and so was probably justified," said a senior trader. "But now stocks are only 100,000 tonnes it needs to be lifted."
The LME was not immediately available for comment.
A further ingredient to the mix is large exposure on LME and over-the-counter (OTC) copper options.
Some market makers and banks are understood to be short of upside call options between $2,300 and $2,600 a tonne.
As the market moves close to or above these strikes, the shorts are likely to cover their exposure by buying increasing quantities of copper futures, fuelling any rally.
Influential traders holding large short option positions may try to keep prices below the strikes near term, traders said, but their task would be more difficult if prices did take off.
